## Research {.section-title}
<hr class="section-rule">

We take a **comparative approach** to understanding human uniqueness, combining biological anthropology, palaeontology, and evolutionary biology to investigate how and why humans and other primates came to look and behave as they do today. Our work draws on a broad methodological toolkit:

```{=html}
<div class="row g-4 mt-3">

  <div class="col-md-6 col-lg-4">
    <div class="research-card">
      <div class="rc-icon">🦴</div>
      <h4>3D Morphometrics &amp; Shape Analysis</h4>
      <p>We use geometric morphometrics and 3D scanning to quantify anatomical variation across
      primates and hominins, identifying patterns of shape change through evolutionary time and
      testing hypotheses about adaptation and constraint. By capturing the geometry of bones in
      fine detail, we can compare skeletal form across species and fossil specimens in ways that
      traditional linear measurements cannot.</p>
      <p style="margin-top:0.8rem;font-size:0.85rem;">
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/ajpa.22882" target="_blank" style="color:var(--accent);">
          Example publication →
        </a>
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="col-md-6 col-lg-4">
    <div class="research-card">
      <div class="rc-icon">⚙️</div>
      <h4>Virtual Computational Biomechanics</h4>
      <p>We use computational modelling — including finite element analysis, musculoskeletal
      simulation, and computational fluid dynamics — to reconstruct the mechanical performance
      of biological structures in living and extinct species. This lets us test functional
      hypotheses about locomotion, feeding, and tool use that cannot be addressed through
      morphology alone, opening a window onto the behaviour of animals known only from fossils.</p>
      <p style="margin-top:0.8rem;font-size:0.85rem;">
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-60590-6" target="_blank" style="color:var(--accent);">
          Example publication →
        </a>
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="col-md-6 col-lg-4">
    <div class="research-card">
      <div class="rc-icon">🌳</div>
      <h4>Phylogenetic Comparative Methods</h4>
      <p>We develop and apply statistical methods for analysing trait evolution along phylogenetic
      trees — estimating divergence times, modelling rates of morphological and life-history
      change, and testing macroevolutionary hypotheses across primates and hominins. By situating
      traits within an explicit evolutionary framework, we can ask not just what changed, but when,
      how fast, and under what selective pressures.</p>
      <p style="margin-top:0.8rem;font-size:0.85rem;">
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3003771" target="_blank" style="color:var(--accent);">
          Example publication →
        </a>
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="col-md-6 col-lg-4">
    <div class="research-card">
      <div class="rc-icon">🧠</div>
      <h4>Human Brain &amp; Body Evolution</h4>
      <p>A major focus is the evolution of encephalization and body size in the hominin lineage —
      including the timing, tempo, and drivers of brain expansion, and what distinguishes
      <em>Homo sapiens</em> from earlier hominins and our primate relatives. We combine
      phylogenetic modelling with the fossil record to understand how and why the human brain
      grew so large, and what ecological and social factors shaped body size across our lineage.</p>
      <p style="margin-top:0.8rem;font-size:0.85rem;">
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2409542121" target="_blank" style="color:var(--accent);">
          Example publication →
        </a>
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="col-md-6 col-lg-4">
    <div class="research-card">
      <div class="rc-icon">🦧</div>
      <h4>Primate Adaptive Evolution</h4>
      <p>We investigate the adaptive radiation of primates — how they diversified into different
      ecological niches, how their locomotor and dietary anatomy evolved, and what drives
      macroevolutionary patterns of diversification and body plan innovation. New World monkeys,
      apes, and fossil primates from across the globe all feature in this work, which integrates
      morphological, biomechanical, and phylogenetic data.</p>
      <p style="margin-top:0.8rem;font-size:0.85rem;">
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2423833122" target="_blank" style="color:var(--accent);">
          Example publication →
        </a>
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="col-md-6 col-lg-4">
    <div class="research-card">
      <div class="rc-icon">🌍</div>
      <h4>Palaeoanthropological Fieldwork</h4>
      <p>We participate in the
      <a href="https://www.gorongosa.org/science/palaeo-primate-project" target="_blank">Palaeo-Primate Project</a>
      in Gorongosa National Park, Mozambique, recovering Miocene fossil primates from
      the southern East African Rift — some of the oldest known from coastal woodland environments.
      This fieldwork grounds our evolutionary questions in the direct evidence of the fossil record.</p>
      <p style="margin-top:0.8rem;font-size:0.85rem;">
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2023.107644" target="_blank" style="color:var(--accent);">
          Example publication →
        </a>
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>

</div>
```
